cards.headline: Port St. Lucie could lose $48 million if property tax amendment passes in November
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie City Manager Jesus Merejo told the City Council the city would lose over $48 million in property taxes over the next two years if Amendment 3 passes in November.
cards.body:
During a summer budget workshop at the Port St. Lucie Community Center on Thursday, City Manager Jesus Merejo told the City Council the city would lose over $48 million in property taxes over the next two years if the item passes in November. To prepare for the potential hit, the city is holding the line on hiring. Port St. Lucie says it won't fund 184 requested positions, worth $28.3 million, including 25 new police officers and parks staff the city had already planned to add this year to keep up with growth at Torino Regional Park and the new BMX facility at Tradition Regional Park.

City employees also won't get a cost-of-living raise in the coming budget. On the capital side, the $7.8 million in canceled projects includes a study for a new interchange connecting Marshall Parkway to I-95, an inclusive playground at McChesney Park, and parking improvements at Riverland Paseo Park, along with construction on a new City Hall and parking garage. Brad Keen, the director of the parks and recreation department, told city councilors the lack of new staff would result in deferred maintenance.

The proposal, known as Amendment 3, is headed to Florida voters on the November 3, 2026 ballot after the Legislature passed it during a June special session. If approved, it would raise the state's homestead exemption from $50,000 to $150,000 starting in January 2027, and to $250,000 in January 2028. Because it's a constitutional amendment, it needs at least 60% approval from voters to pass. Scott Samples with the city said the council will reconvene shortly after the November 3rd election to determine next steps.

Chris DuPlessis, Director of Fun for P1 Motor Club, said the club is designed for drivers of all ages and skill levels, from kids as young as 8 years old driving go-karts to grandparents. Developers say they want to preserve the character of the region by planting trees, creating lakes, and incorporating natural landscaping throughout the property. cards.headline: Port St. Lucie bans gas station on Tradition commercial site after months of resident concerns
cards.teaser: The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a permanent ban on gas stations at a 9.4-acre commercial parcel at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Driv
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a permanent ban on gas stations at a 9.4-acre commercial parcel at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Drive on July 13. The restriction came after months of debate over a request by Winding River Crosstown LLC to convert what had been planned as Phase 3 of the Heritage Oaks at Tradition residential development into commercial property. While council members supported adding commercial uses to the rapidly growing area, several voiced concerns during the initial May 26 hearing that a convenience store with gas pumps would worsen traffic along Crosstown Parkway west of Interstate 95.

 The council tabled the request in May after Vice Mayor Jolien Caraballo and other council members asked staff to determine whether gas stations could be eliminated as a permitted use on the parcel. When the hearing resumed June 22, several Heritage Oaks residents urged the council to reject the land-use change, citing concerns about increased traffic, noise and neighborhood impacts. The council voted 4-0 to approve the commercial designation on first reading after the developer agreed to permanently relinquish the right to build a gas station.

 The updated development plan now specifies that while service stations remain permitted elsewhere within the Tradition mixed-use area, they are prohibited on Parcel 11A. The city also added protections requested by nearby residents. Before any mass grading begins, the developer must install a fence along the southern property line to prevent construction access through Southwest Glenbrook Drive, which connects to Heritage Oaks. An architectural wall and landscape buffering must be completed along the southeastern and southern boundaries before the first building permit is issued for vertical construction.

 City planner Bridget Kean confirmed the restriction is now written directly into the Tradition Master Planned Unit Development documents, ensuring no future owner can develop a gas station on the parcel. Councilman Anthony Bonna said he believes expanding commercial development will benefit residents by broadening the city's tax base. Councilman David Pickett said going to commercial is the best possible thing for that corner. The amendment changes the parcel's designation from residential to commercial, paving the way for retail and office development.

"Something I learned after day one is hydration packs, good for hydration obviously but if you fill it up with ice it's good for keeping you cold as well," Weedall said.

"Even when my legs are hurting, even when the traffic is big or even when I'm a little anxious about what's going on around me, but I'm largely just thinking about my friend who doesn't get the opportunity to do this with me anymore," Weedall said. He will ride roughly 150 miles a day up the coast through nearly every state before completing the Pan Mass Challenge across Massachusetts on August 2. Fans can follow his journey on the cycling app Strava.
